title: Design Characteristics of Studies Reporting the Performance of Artificial Intelligence Algorithms for Diagnostic Analysis of Medical Images: Results from Recently Published Papers
explain_beginner: This paper looked at 516 studies from 2018 that tested AI programs for diagnosing medical images. Only 31 studies, about 6 percent, checked their results using data from outside the original setting. None of those 31 also used a patient group that reflects real clinical practice, data from several hospitals, and data gathered going forward in time. The authors conclude that almost all studies were early technical tests, not strong evidence that the AI works in real care. This matters because doctors and buyers should be careful before trusting such tools.
explain_business: For executives considering AI tools for medical imaging, this review suggests the published evidence base from early 2018 was mostly early stage. Among 516 studies, only 6 percent tested performance on data from outside the original development setting. None of those 31 outside validation studies also met all three recommended design features for real world clinical evidence. There was no meaningful difference between medical and non medical journals. The practical decision is to treat most such studies as technical feasibility signals, not proof of clinical readiness, and to ask for stronger validation before clinical use.
explain_practitioner: The authors searched PubMed MEDLINE and Embase for original articles published between January and August 2018 on AI algorithms that diagnose medical images. They assessed whether each study used outside validation, collected validation data, used a diagnostic cohort rather than a case control design, included several institutions, and collected data prospectively. Of 516 eligible studies, 31, or 6 percent, used outside validation. None of those 31 met all three further design features: cohort design, multiple sites, and prospective collection. Medical and non medical journals did not differ significantly. Most work was proof of concept technical feasibility.
